title: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Flight and size”. Scope: large birds, including ratites

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Biomechanical feasibility can be estimated with public scans and comparative traits, especially for the man-sized prediction. The categorical historical claims remain sensitive to uncertain soft tissues and what counts as ordinary anatomy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct body mass, wing area, muscle capacity and required flight power for ostrich, moa and comparably large flying birds, then test whether required power exceeds physiologically plausible muscle output under ordinary avian anatomy. A feasible positive power margin would refute physiological impossibility.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Moa soft tissue and wing anatomy require uncertain reconstruction.

Extant ratites' reduced wings reflect evolutionary history as well as size.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Extant bird proportions and a biomechanical threshold make the man-sized and ostrich clauses testable in outline, and moa occurrences are in a public fossil database. The impossibility criterion is model-dependent, moa wing area is poorly known because the wings are reduced, and small flightless birds show that loss of flight is not diagnostic of having passed a size limit. The data resolve a restricted biomechanical version, not the historical claim that size is why these birds cannot fly.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare required flight power with plausible muscle power at the masses and wing plans of the ostrich, moa, the heaviest flying birds, and a bird of about human mass with ordinary avian proportions. The claim is supported if moa and the man-sized bird lie beyond muscle power and the ostrich is marginal; it is weakened if birds of those masses fly with ordinary avian muscle fractions and wing shapes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Flightlessness also evolves in birds far below any aerodynamic ceiling.

Moa mass and wing reduction are fossil estimates with wide error.

The ostrich clause is explicitly probable rather than certain.
